title: Cleartext Database Protocol (No TLS/SSL)
description: The database is accepting connections without TLS/SSL encryption. All data transmitted between client and server, including credentials and query results, is exposed to network interception.
remediation: Enable TLS/SSL encryption for all database connections. Configure the database server to require encrypted connections and update all clients to use SSL. For MySQL: set require_secure_transport=ON. For PostgreSQL: set ssl=on in postgresql.conf and hostssl in pg_hba.conf. For MSSQL: enable Force Encryption in SQL Server Configuration Manager.

title: Weak TLS Version (TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1)
description: The database accepts connections using deprecated TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1. These versions have known vulnerabilities including POODLE and BEAST attacks. PCI DSS explicitly prohibits TLS 1.0 and early TLS in cardholder data environments.
remediation: Disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1. Configure the database to accept only TLS 1.2 or higher. Update cipher suites to exclude RC4, 3DES, and export cipher suites.

title: Self-Signed or Expired TLS Certificate
description: The database is using a self-signed or expired TLS certificate. Self-signed certificates cannot be verified against a trusted certificate authority, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks by clients configured to accept any certificate.
remediation: Replace the self-signed or expired certificate with one issued by a trusted internal or public certificate authority. Implement automated certificate renewal (e.g., Let's Encrypt, AWS ACM) to prevent expiry. Configure clients to validate server certificates.

title: Database Listening on All Network Interfaces (0.0.0.0)
description: The database is configured to listen on all network interfaces (0.0.0.0). This unnecessarily exposes the database port on all network interfaces, including public-facing ones, significantly increasing the attack surface.
remediation: Configure the database to bind only to required interfaces. For most deployments, bind to the loopback (127.0.0.1) or the specific private IP the application uses. Apply firewall rules to restrict access to the database port to authorized source IPs only.
validation_notes: Verify the actual network exposure using: ss -tlnp | grep <port> or netstat -tlnp | grep <port>. Also check firewall rules: iptables -L -n | grep <port> or ufw status numbered.

title: Audit Logging Disabled
description: Database audit logging is disabled or not configured. Without audit logging, there is no record of database access, query execution, privilege changes, or schema modifications. This prevents detection of unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or insider threats.
remediation: Enable comprehensive audit logging. At minimum, log: authentication attempts (success and failure), privileged operations, schema changes (DDL), data access to sensitive tables, and configuration changes. Ensure logs are shipped to an external SIEM and protected from modification.

title: Default Credentials in Use
description: The database is accessible using well-known default credentials. Default credentials are widely documented and the first credentials attempted in automated attacks. Successful authentication with default credentials grants an attacker immediate access to all data accessible by that account.
remediation: Immediately change all default passwords to strong, unique credentials. Disable or remove default accounts that are not required. Implement a credential rotation policy and use a secrets manager to store database credentials securely.

title: Database Accessible Without Authentication
description: The database accepts connections without requiring authentication. Any client with network access to the database port can connect and access data without providing credentials.
remediation: Immediately enable authentication. Every database connection must require valid credentials. Apply network-level controls (firewall, VPC security groups) as a secondary defense, but authentication must be the primary control.

title: Database Service Running as Root or Administrator
description: The database service process is running under a root or administrator account. If the database is compromised, an attacker would gain full operating system access, enabling lateral movement, privilege escalation, and complete system compromise.
remediation: Run the database service under a dedicated, least-privilege service account. The service account should have no interactive login capability, no write access outside the database data directory, and no sudo privileges.
validation_notes: Verify the OS user running the database process: ps aux | grep <db_process> or systemctl show <service_name> --property User. Check the user's group memberships: id <username>.

title: End-of-Life Database Version
description: The database is running an end-of-life (EOL) version that no longer receives security patches from the vendor. Vulnerabilities discovered after the EOL date will never be patched, leaving the database permanently vulnerable.
remediation: Upgrade to a supported version of the database software. Plan a migration path that includes testing, backup, and rollback procedures. Subscribe to vendor security advisories to stay informed of future EOL dates.

title: Known CVE in Installed Database Version
description: The installed database version contains one or more published CVEs. The exact risk depends on the specific CVEs identified.
remediation: Apply available vendor patches or upgrade to a patched version. Evaluate each CVE for applicability to your configuration and implement compensating controls where immediate patching is not possible.
validation_notes: Validate with: searchsploit <db_type> <version>, or query NVD: curl 'https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?keywordSearch=<db_type>+<version>'. Also check: https://www.cvedetails.com/

title: Overprivileged Database User Account
description: One or more database user accounts have been granted privileges beyond what is required for their function (violation of the principle of least privilege). Overprivileged accounts increase the blast radius of a compromised account.
remediation: Audit all user accounts and their privileges. Remove all unnecessary grants. Implement role-based access control (RBAC) and assign users to minimal-privilege roles. Application accounts should have DML (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on specific required tables only — never DDL or admin privileges.

title: Dormant / Inactive User Account
description: One or more database user accounts have not been used for an extended period (>90 days). Dormant accounts represent an attack surface: if compromised, they may go unnoticed longer than active accounts, and their passwords may not be rotated.
remediation: Disable or remove accounts inactive for more than 90 days (or per your security policy). Implement account lifecycle management to automatically disable accounts after a defined inactivity period. Review all service and shared accounts to confirm they are still required.
validation_notes: Verify last login by checking database-specific last_login columns or audit log timestamps. For MySQL: SELECT user, host, password_last_changed FROM mysql.user. For PostgreSQL check pg_stat_activity history via audit logs.

title: Password Policy Not Enforced
description: The database does not enforce a password complexity, length, or history policy. Without a password policy, users can set trivially weak passwords that are easily brute-forced.
remediation: Enable the database's password validation plugin/policy and configure minimum length (12+ characters), complexity requirements (upper, lower, digit, special), password history (prevent reuse of last 12 passwords), and maximum password age (90 days or per policy).

title: Account Lockout Policy Not Configured
description: No account lockout or rate-limiting policy is configured. Without lockout, an attacker can attempt unlimited password guesses against database accounts without consequence.
remediation: Configure account lockout after 5-10 failed authentication attempts. Set a lockout duration of at least 30 minutes or require administrator unlock. Ensure lockout applies to all authentication methods including service accounts.

title: Sensitive Data Columns Identified (Potential PII/PHI/PCI Scope)
description: Column names matching patterns associated with sensitive data (PII, PHI, or payment card data) were identified. This finding indicates potential scope for data protection regulations and requires validation to confirm whether actual sensitive data is stored.
remediation: Review identified columns to confirm the nature of stored data. Apply appropriate controls: encryption at rest (TDE, column-level encryption), access controls limiting visibility to authorized users, data masking for non-production environments, and compliance classification tagging.
validation_notes: Validate by sampling data from flagged columns. Check for encryption: SELECT TOP 1 * FROM <table> WHERE <sensitive_col> IS NOT NULL. Verify if TDE is enabled. Review column-level permissions and access patterns in audit logs.

title: Encryption at Rest Not Configured
description: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) or equivalent at-rest encryption is not enabled. If physical storage media is stolen or a backup is exfiltrated, data is readable without additional decryption.
remediation: Enable TDE or filesystem-level encryption for the database data directory. For MySQL: enable InnoDB tablespace encryption. For MSSQL: enable TDE. For PostgreSQL: use pgcrypto or filesystem encryption. Protect encryption keys in a dedicated key management service (KMS).
validation_notes: For MSSQL: SELECT * FROM sys.dm_database_encryption_keys. For MySQL: SELECT * FROM information_schema.INNODB_TABLESPACES_ENCRYPTION. For Oracle: SELECT * FROM v$encryption_wallet.

title: Weak Cipher Suites Accepted
description: The database TLS configuration accepts weak or deprecated cipher suites including RC4, DES, 3DES, export ciphers, or anonymous key exchange. These ciphers have known weaknesses that can be exploited to decrypt traffic.
remediation: Configure the database TLS stack to accept only strong cipher suites: AES-128/256-GCM, CHACHA20-POLY1305 with ECDHE key exchange. Disable: RC4, DES, 3DES, EXPORT, NULL, ANON ciphers. Follow NIST SP 800-52 Rev 2 for approved cipher suites.

title: Verbose Error Messages Enabled
description: The database is configured to return verbose error messages that may reveal internal configuration details, version information, file paths, or query structure to clients. This information aids attackers in crafting targeted attacks.
remediation: Configure error reporting to use minimal/generic error messages for client-facing errors. Log detailed error information server-side only. For application-facing databases, errors should be handled at the application layer before reaching end users.

title: Remote Code Execution Feature Enabled
description: A feature capable of executing operating system commands or arbitrary code is enabled. This includes features such as xp_cmdshell (MSSQL), UTL_FILE/UTL_HTTP (Oracle), UDFs calling shared libraries (MySQL), or eval/execute (JavaScript in document stores). If an attacker gains SQL access, they can immediately pivot to OS-level code execution.
remediation: Disable all features that allow database queries to execute operating system commands or load external code. These should never be enabled in production. If genuinely required, restrict execution to specific stored procedures callable only by administrator accounts, with all calls logged and alerted.

title: Shared Service Account Used by Multiple Applications
description: Multiple applications appear to be using the same database service account. Shared accounts prevent proper attribution of database activity, complicate least-privilege implementation, and mean that compromising one application exposes all applications sharing the account.
remediation: Create dedicated service accounts for each application with only the permissions that application requires. This enables granular audit trails, least-privilege enforcement, and limits blast radius when an application is compromised.
validation_notes: Review connection sources in audit logs or active sessions: SHOW PROCESSLIST (MySQL), SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity (PostgreSQL), SELECT * FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions (MSSQL). Correlate application connections to source IPs to identify shared account usage.

title: MySQL: Anonymous User Account Present
description: One or more anonymous (blank username) user accounts exist in the MySQL user table. Anonymous accounts allow any client to connect to the database without credentials. Even if the anonymous account has limited permissions, its existence creates an unauthenticated access path.
remediation: Remove all anonymous accounts: DROP USER ''@'localhost'; DROP USER ''@'%'; Verify removal: SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user WHERE user=''; Run FLUSH PRIVILEGES after removal.

title: MySQL: Test Database Present and Accessible
description: The MySQL 'test' database is present and accessible. The 'test' database is created by default during MySQL installation. Anonymous users often have access to this database, and it may be used to store temporary data or exploit MySQL features like SELECT INTO OUTFILE.
remediation: Drop the test database: DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS test; Remove any permissions on the test database: DELETE FROM mysql.db WHERE Db='test' OR Db='test\_%'; FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

title: MySQL: LOCAL INFILE Enabled
description: The MySQL global variable local_infile is enabled. This allows LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE to read files from the client filesystem and send them to the server. A malicious MySQL server can abuse this to read arbitrary files from any connecting client. Attackers who can man-in-the-middle a MySQL connection can abuse this to exfiltrate client-side sensitive files.
remediation: Disable local_infile: SET GLOBAL local_infile = OFF; Persist in my.cnf: [mysqld] local_infile=0. Also configure connecting clients with --ssl-mode=REQUIRED and --local-infile=0 to protect against malicious server attacks.

title: MySQL: secure_file_priv Not Configured
description: The MySQL secure_file_priv variable is empty or not configured, allowing SELECT INTO OUTFILE and LOAD DATA INFILE to read and write files from any location accessible by the MySQL service account. This can be used to read sensitive files or write web shells.
remediation: Set secure_file_priv to a dedicated, non-web-accessible directory, or set it to NULL to disable file operations entirely. In my.cnf: secure_file_priv=/var/lib/mysql-files/ (ensure this directory is not web-accessible and not sensitive). Setting secure_file_priv='' or leaving it unset is the vulnerable state.

title: MySQL: Root Account Accessible Remotely
description: The MySQL root account has a remote host wildcard (%) or specific remote host entry allowing remote connections. The root account has unrestricted access to all databases and MySQL system tables. Remote root access is a severe security risk.
remediation: Restrict the root account to localhost only: UPDATE mysql.user SET host='localhost' WHERE user='root' AND host!='localhost'; DELETE FROM mysql.user WHERE user='root' AND host!='localhost'; FLUSH PRIVILEGES; For remote administration, use SSH tunneling to connect to localhost.

title: MySQL: User Account with Wildcard Host (%)
description: One or more MySQL user accounts have a host value of '%', allowing connections from any remote IP address. Combined with weak passwords or network exposure, wildcard host entries enable brute-force attacks from anywhere on the internet.
remediation: Replace wildcard host entries with specific IP addresses or CIDR ranges. Update user host: RENAME USER 'user'@'%' TO 'user'@'10.0.1.%'; or restrict to localhost where remote access is not needed. Apply firewall rules as a secondary control.

title: MySQL: Password Validation Plugin Not Installed
description: The MySQL validate_password plugin (MySQL 5.7) or component (MySQL 8.0+) is not installed or is configured with insufficient policy strength. Without this, users can set trivially weak passwords.
remediation: Install and configure the password validation component. For MySQL 8.0+: INSTALL COMPONENT 'file://component_validate_password'; SET GLOBAL validate_password.policy=STRONG; SET GLOBAL validate_password.length=12; SET GLOBAL validate_password.mixed_case_count=1; SET GLOBAL validate_password.number_count=1; SET GLOBAL validate_password.special_char_count=1;

title: MySQL: General Query Log Enabled (Production Risk)
description: The MySQL general query log is enabled. The general log records all statements sent to the server including queries containing passwords and sensitive data. In production environments this creates a sensitive data exposure risk and significant I/O overhead.
remediation: Disable the general query log in production: SET GLOBAL general_log = 'OFF'; If query logging is required for troubleshooting, enable it temporarily with a defined time window and ensure log files are properly secured and not stored on web-accessible volumes.

title: MySQL: Symlink Support Enabled
description: MySQL symbolic link support is enabled (have_symlink = YES). MySQL can follow symlinks when accessing table files, potentially allowing an attacker with FILE privilege to access or replace files outside the MySQL data directory.
remediation: Disable symlink support in my.cnf: [mysqld] skip-symbolic-links. Verify: SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'have_symlink'; should return DISABLED.

title: MySQL: Replication Account with Overly Broad Privileges
description: A MySQL account with REPLICATION SLAVE or REPLICATION CLIENT privileges has been granted additional privileges beyond what is required for replication. Replication accounts should be limited to only replication-related privileges.
remediation: Create dedicated replication accounts with only REPLICATION SLAVE privilege: CREATE USER 'replicator'@'replica_ip' IDENTIFIED BY 'strong_password'; GRANT REPLICATION SLAVE ON *.* TO 'replicator'@'replica_ip'; Revoke any additional privileges granted to replication accounts.

title: MySQL: sql_mode Too Permissive (NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES Missing)
description: MySQL sql_mode does not include NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES or STRICT_ALL_TABLES. A permissive sql_mode allows invalid data to be silently truncated or coerced, and the absence of NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES can affect SQL injection protection in some application escaping implementations.
remediation: Configure a strict and secure sql_mode. Recommended: STRICT_TRANS_TABLES,NO_ZERO_IN_DATE,NO_ZERO_DATE,ERROR_FOR_DIVISION_BY_ZERO,NO_ENGINE_SUBSTITUTION,NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES. Set in my.cnf: sql_mode=<value>.

title: PostgreSQL: Trust Authentication in pg_hba.conf
description: PostgreSQL pg_hba.conf contains one or more 'trust' authentication entries. Trust authentication allows any client matching the host/database pattern to connect without providing a password. This is a critical authentication bypass vulnerability.
remediation: Replace all 'trust' entries in pg_hba.conf with 'scram-sha-256' or 'md5' (scram-sha-256 is strongly preferred for PostgreSQL 10+). Reload configuration: SELECT pg_reload_conf(); Verify no trust entries remain: grep 'trust' /etc/postgresql/*/main/pg_hba.conf

title: PostgreSQL: Superuser Account Accessible Remotely
description: A PostgreSQL superuser account (has usesuper=true) is configured for remote access in pg_hba.conf. Superusers bypass all access controls. Remote superuser access dramatically increases the risk of full database compromise.
remediation: Restrict superuser connections to local sockets in pg_hba.conf. Create named role accounts for DBA tasks without the SUPERUSER attribute. For remote DBA work, use SSH tunneling to connect via local socket: ssh -L 5432:localhost:5432 dba@server, then psql -h localhost.

title: PostgreSQL: COPY TO/FROM PROGRAM Feature Accessible
description: The PostgreSQL superuser can execute: COPY ... FROM PROGRAM 'command', which executes arbitrary OS commands as the postgres service user. If an attacker gains superuser access, this provides immediate OS code execution. All pg_read_server_files / pg_write_server_files roles also have file I/O.
remediation: Restrict pg_execute_server_program, pg_read_server_files, and pg_write_server_files membership to only accounts that absolutely require it. Ensure no application service accounts hold superuser. Monitor/alert on COPY FROM PROGRAM usage in audit logs.

title: PostgreSQL: Row-Level Security (RLS) Not Enabled on Sensitive Tables
description: Tables that appear to contain sensitive data do not have Row-Level Security (RLS) enabled. Without RLS, any user with SELECT privilege on a table can read all rows, including rows belonging to other users or tenants. RLS is a critical control for multi-tenant applications and PII/PHI data stores.
remediation: Enable RLS on sensitive tables: ALTER TABLE <table> ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE <table> FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; Create appropriate policies: CREATE POLICY <policy_name> ON <table> USING (owner_id = current_user_id()); Apply to all users by default (FORCE RLS overrides table owners).
validation_notes: Check which tables have sensitive data but no RLS: SELECT schemaname, tablename, rowsecurity FROM pg_tables WHERE rowsecurity = false; Cross-reference with table names matching PII/PHI patterns.

title: PostgreSQL: Weak Password Encryption (MD5 Instead of SCRAM-SHA-256)
description: PostgreSQL password_encryption is set to 'md5'. MD5 is a weak password hashing algorithm vulnerable to rainbow table and brute-force attacks. PostgreSQL 10+ supports SCRAM-SHA-256 which is significantly more secure.
remediation: Change password encryption to scram-sha-256 in postgresql.conf: password_encryption = scram-sha-256. Update pg_hba.conf to use scram-sha-256. Force all users to change passwords: ALTER USER <username> PASSWORD '<new_password>'; This will re-hash using the new algorithm.

title: PostgreSQL: Excessive Permissions on Public Schema
description: The PostgreSQL public schema has CREATE privilege granted to PUBLIC (all users). This allows any database user to create objects in the public schema, enabling privilege escalation via search_path manipulation (CVE-2018-1058). An attacker can create a function with the same name as a built-in, causing it to be called in trusted contexts.
remediation: Revoke CREATE on the public schema from PUBLIC: REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC; Set a safe default search_path: ALTER DATABASE <dbname> SET search_path = '$user'; Ensure application service accounts use dedicated schemas rather than the public schema.

title: PostgreSQL: Connection Logging Disabled
description: PostgreSQL is not configured to log connection attempts, disconnections, or failed authentication. Without connection logging, there is no record of who connected to the database, when, and from where, preventing detection of unauthorized access.
remediation: Configure in postgresql.conf: log_connections = on, log_disconnections = on, log_failed_attempts = on (if supported), log_min_duration_statement = 1000 (log slow queries), log_line_prefix = '%t [%p]: [%l-1] user=%u,db=%d,app=%a,client=%h '. Reload: SELECT pg_reload_conf();

title: PostgreSQL: Dangerous Extensions Installed
description: One or more potentially dangerous PostgreSQL extensions are installed that provide file system access, network access, or OS command execution capabilities: dblink, postgres_fdw, pg_read_file, plsh, plpython, plperl. If an attacker gains database access, these extensions can be used to further compromise the system.
remediation: Remove extensions that are not required: DROP EXTENSION IF EXISTS <extension_name>; For required extensions (e.g., plpgsql), restrict EXECUTE permission: REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION <function> FROM PUBLIC; Ensure only trusted roles (not application service accounts) have access to these extensions.
validation_notes: Review installed extensions: SELECT name, default_version, installed_version FROM pg_available_extensions WHERE installed_version IS NOT NULL ORDER BY name; Assess whether each extension is operationally required.

title: MSSQL: xp_cmdshell Enabled
description: The SQL Server xp_cmdshell extended stored procedure is enabled. xp_cmdshell spawns a Windows command shell and passes a string for execution, returning any output as rows of text. Any SQL user with EXECUTE permission on xp_cmdshell can run arbitrary OS commands as the SQL Server service account.
remediation: Disable xp_cmdshell: EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options', 1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell', 0; RECONFIGURE; There is almost never a legitimate reason to have xp_cmdshell enabled in production. Audit all stored procedures that reference xp_cmdshell.

title: MSSQL: SA Account Enabled
description: The SQL Server 'sa' (System Administrator) built-in account is enabled. The 'sa' account is the most well-known SQL Server account and is targeted by automated attacks. It has unrestricted sysadmin access to all SQL Server instances.
remediation: Disable the sa account: ALTER LOGIN sa DISABLE; Rename it as an additional deterrent: ALTER LOGIN sa WITH NAME = [sqladmin_$(random)]; Use named administrator accounts for DBA operations with individual accountability. Never use sa for application connections.

title: MSSQL: CLR Integration Enabled
description: SQL Server Common Language Runtime (CLR) integration is enabled. CLR allows .NET assemblies to run inside SQL Server. UNSAFE assemblies can call arbitrary .NET code including OS APIs, networking, and file system operations. Attackers with sysadmin can load malicious CLR assemblies for persistence and code execution.
remediation: Disable CLR integration if not required: EXEC sp_configure 'clr enabled', 0; RECONFIGURE; If CLR is required, allow only SAFE assemblies and audit all installed assemblies: SELECT * FROM sys.assemblies; Restrict CREATE ASSEMBLY permission to DBA roles only.

title: MSSQL: OLE Automation Procedures Enabled
description: OLE Automation Procedures (sp_OACreate, sp_OAMethod, etc.) are enabled. These allow instantiation of COM/OLE objects from T-SQL, enabling file system access, network operations, and arbitrary code execution. Combined with sysadmin access, these procedures provide OS-level code execution.
remediation: Disable OLE Automation: EXEC sp_configure 'Ole Automation Procedures', 0; RECONFIGURE; This feature should never be enabled in production. Audit existing stored procedures for OLE Automation usage before disabling.

title: MSSQL: Linked Servers Configured
description: One or more SQL Server Linked Servers are configured. Linked Servers allow query execution on remote databases from T-SQL. If configured with stored credentials, compromising the SQL instance grants access to all linked servers. Linked servers are a common lateral movement vector.
remediation: Review all linked servers and remove those that are not actively required: EXEC sp_dropserver '<linked_server_name>', 'droplogins'; For required linked servers, use 'Not Be Made' (impersonation) rather than stored passwords, and restrict EXECUTE permissions on linked server procedures to specific service accounts.

title: MSSQL: Mixed Mode Authentication with SQL Logins Not Subject to Password Policy
description: SQL Server is running in mixed-mode authentication (both Windows and SQL authentication), and one or more SQL logins are not subject to the Windows password policy (is_policy_checked = 0) or password expiration (is_expiration_checked = 0). These accounts can retain weak or non-expiring passwords indefinitely.
remediation: Enable password policy checking on all SQL logins: ALTER LOGIN <login_name> WITH CHECK_POLICY = ON, CHECK_EXPIRATION = ON; Prefer Windows Authentication over SQL authentication. For SQL logins that must exist, enforce strong passwords and policy compliance.

title: MSSQL: BUILTIN\Administrators in Sysadmin Role
description: The BUILTIN\Administrators Windows group is a member of the SQL Server sysadmin fixed server role. This means any local Windows administrator automatically has unrestricted sysadmin access to SQL Server. This is a critical privilege escalation path: any user with local admin becomes a SQL Server sysadmin.
remediation: Remove BUILTIN\Administrators from sysadmin: EXEC sp_dropsrvrolemember 'BUILTIN\Administrators', 'sysadmin'; Create explicit Windows group or user mappings for SQL Server administration: CREATE LOGIN [DOMAIN\SQLAdmins] FROM WINDOWS; EXEC sp_addsrvrolemember 'DOMAIN\SQLAdmins', 'sysadmin';

title: MSSQL: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) Not Enabled
description: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) is not enabled on one or more databases. Without TDE, database files (MDF, LDF, NDF) and backups stored on disk are unencrypted. Physical media theft or unauthorized backup access would expose all data in plaintext.
remediation: Enable TDE on all databases containing sensitive data: CREATE DATABASE ENCRYPTION KEY WITH ALGORITHM = AES_256 ENCRYPTION BY SERVER CERTIFICATE <cert_name>; ALTER DATABASE <database_name> SET ENCRYPTION ON; Ensure the database encryption key (DEK) certificate is backed up securely and stored separately from the data.

title: MSSQL: Ad Hoc Distributed Queries Enabled
description: Ad Hoc Distributed Queries are enabled, allowing the use of OPENROWSET and OPENDATASOURCE to access remote data sources from T-SQL. An attacker with sufficient SQL privileges can use these to access remote SMB shares (NTLM hash capture) or OLE DB data sources.
remediation: Disable Ad Hoc Distributed Queries: EXEC sp_configure 'Ad Hoc Distributed Queries', 0; RECONFIGURE; If remote data access is required, use properly configured Linked Servers with least-privilege credentials instead.

title: Oracle: Accounts Using Default Passwords
description: Oracle database accounts are using their default passwords as installed. Oracle installs dozens of pre-seeded accounts with well-known default passwords (SYS/change_on_install, SYSTEM/manager, SCOTT/tiger, HR/hr, etc.). These are the first credentials attempted by attackers and automated tools.
remediation: Change all default passwords immediately. Oracle 11g+: use the DBA_USERS_WITH_DEFPWD view to identify accounts with default passwords: SELECT username FROM dba_users_with_defpwd; For Oracle 12c+: use mandatory profile PASSWORD_VERIFY_FUNCTION to enforce complexity. Lock all accounts not required for operation: ALTER USER <username> ACCOUNT LOCK;

title: Oracle: PUBLIC Role Has Execute on Dangerous Packages
description: The PUBLIC role has EXECUTE privilege on one or more potentially dangerous Oracle packages: UTL_FILE (file I/O), UTL_HTTP (network requests), UTL_TCP/UTL_SMTP (network), DBMS_JAVA (JVM code execution), UTL_INADDR (hostname resolution). Any database user inherits PUBLIC role privileges, so any authenticated user can use these packages.
remediation: Revoke PUBLIC execute on dangerous packages: REVOKE EXECUTE ON UTL_FILE FROM PUBLIC; REVOKE EXECUTE ON UTL_HTTP FROM PUBLIC; REVOKE EXECUTE ON DBMS_JAVA FROM PUBLIC; REVOKE EXECUTE ON UTL_TCP FROM PUBLIC; Grant execute only to specific schemas that legitimately require it.

title: Oracle: Unified Auditing Not Enabled
description: Oracle Unified Auditing is not enabled or not configured with comprehensive policies. Without unified auditing, privileged operations, schema changes, failed logins, and data access are not recorded in a tamper-evident audit trail.
remediation: Enable Unified Auditing (Oracle 12c+): Link Oracle binary with unified auditing enabled (requires relink). Create audit policies: CREATE AUDIT POLICY all_actions ACTIONS ALL; AUDIT POLICY all_actions; At minimum audit: CREATE SESSION, ALTER DATABASE, DROP TABLE, EXECUTE on sensitive packages, privileged user activity.

title: Oracle: Oracle Label Security (OLS) Not Configured
oracle_ols: OLS mandatory access control not applied
description: Oracle Label Security (OLS) is available but not configured. OLS provides mandatory access control (MAC) enabling row-level security based on sensitivity labels. For environments processing classified or highly sensitive data (government, healthcare, financial), OLS ensures that users can only access data at or below their security clearance level.
remediation: Evaluate whether OLS is appropriate for the data classification requirements. To configure OLS: EXEC LBACSYS.SA_SYSDBA.CREATE_POLICY('policy_name', 'label_column_name'); Define label components (levels, compartments, groups). Apply the policy to sensitive tables. Assign user labels matching their access requirements.
validation_notes: Check if OLS is installed: SELECT * FROM dba_ols_policies; Check if any tables have OLS policies applied: SELECT * FROM dba_ols_table_policies; Assess data sensitivity to determine if mandatory access control is warranted.

title: Oracle: Default Profile Has No Password Expiry
description: The Oracle DEFAULT user profile has PASSWORD_LIFE_TIME = UNLIMITED, allowing users on the default profile to retain the same password indefinitely. Without password expiry, compromised credentials may be used indefinitely without detection or rotation.
remediation: Modify the DEFAULT profile: ALTER PROFILE DEFAULT LIMIT PASSWORD_LIFE_TIME 90 PASSWORD_REUSE_TIME 365 PASSWORD_REUSE_MAX 10 FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS 5 PASSWORD_LOCK_TIME 1/24 PASSWORD_GRACE_TIME 7; Create purpose-specific profiles for service accounts with appropriate limits.

title: Oracle: Data Dictionary Protection Disabled
description: Oracle O7_DICTIONARY_ACCESSIBILITY is set to TRUE, allowing users with ANY privilege (e.g., SELECT ANY TABLE) to access the data dictionary (sys-owned tables/views). This violates the principle of dictionary protection and can be used to bypass security policies.
remediation: Disable dictionary accessibility: ALTER SYSTEM SET O7_DICTIONARY_ACCESSIBILITY=FALSE SCOPE=SPFILE; Restart the database. Verify: SHOW PARAMETER O7_DICTIONARY_ACCESSIBILITY. Remove ANY-style system privileges from non-DBA accounts.

title: MongoDB: Authentication Disabled
description: MongoDB is running without authentication enabled (--noauth or security.authorization not set in mongod.conf). Any client with network access can connect and read/write all databases without credentials. This is the single most critical MongoDB misconfiguration and has led to numerous large-scale data breaches.
remediation: Enable authentication immediately. In mongod.conf: security: authorization: enabled. Create admin user first: use admin; db.createUser({user:'admin',pwd:'<strong_password>',roles:[{role:'userAdminAnyDatabase',db:'admin'}]}). Create least-privilege application accounts: db.createUser({user:'app',pwd:'<password>',roles:[{role:'readWrite',db:'app_db'}]}). Restart with --auth flag.

title: MongoDB: Server-Side JavaScript Execution Enabled
description: MongoDB is configured with server-side JavaScript execution enabled (security.javascriptEnabled = true). Server-side JavaScript via $where, mapReduce, $function, and group() can be exploited for NoSQL injection attacks if not properly sanitized, and consumes significant resources enabling DoS via complex JS execution.
remediation: Disable server-side JavaScript: in mongod.conf: security: javascriptEnabled: false. Review all application queries for $where, mapReduce, and group() usage and replace with MongoDB aggregation pipeline equivalents. With authentication enabled and JS disabled, the attack surface is significantly reduced.

title: MongoDB: No TLS/SSL Configured
description: MongoDB is not configured with TLS/SSL encryption for client connections. All data, including authentication credentials and query results, is transmitted in cleartext.
remediation: Configure TLS in mongod.conf: net: tls: mode: requireTLS certificateKeyFile: /etc/mongodb/server.pem CAFile: /etc/mongodb/ca.pem. For clients, require TLS: --tls --tlsCAFile ca.pem. Generate certificates from an internal CA or use Let's Encrypt. Do not use allowTLS or preferTLS in production — use requireTLS.

title: MongoDB: User with Root or __system Role
description: One or more MongoDB users have the 'root' or '__system' built-in role. The 'root' role combines the privileges of all other roles and provides full unrestricted access. The '__system' role is for internal MongoDB use only and grants the ability to take any action on any resource.
remediation: Remove root/__system roles from non-DBA accounts. Replace with specific database roles (readWrite, dbAdmin, etc.). For DBA accounts, use userAdminAnyDatabase and dbAdminAnyDatabase instead of root. Application service accounts should never have root or __system privileges.

title: MongoDB: Oplog Readable by Application Accounts
description: Application-level user accounts have read access to the MongoDB oplog (operations log in the local database). The oplog contains a record of all write operations including the full data before and after each change. Reading the oplog enables data exfiltration of all historical writes.
remediation: Restrict oplog access to replication accounts only. Application service accounts should only have read/write access to their specific databases. Remove local.oplog.rs read access: REVOKE clusterMonitor role or remove readOplog role. Review all accounts that have local database access.
validation_notes: Test oplog access: db.getSiblingDB('local').oplog.rs.find().limit(5). If this returns data from an application account, the account has oplog access. Review account roles for any inherited oplog permissions.

title: Redis: No Authentication Configured (requirepass Not Set)
description: Redis is running without a password (requirepass is not configured). Any client with network access to the Redis port can execute any Redis command including FLUSHALL (delete all data), CONFIG (modify server configuration), SLAVEOF (initiate replication to attacker-controlled server), and DEBUG SLEEP (DoS).
remediation: Set a strong password in redis.conf: requirepass <strong_128bit_plus_password>. Redis v6+: implement ACL (Access Control Lists) instead of requirepass for granular per-user command restrictions: ACL SETUSER appuser on ><password> ~* +@read +@write -CONFIG -FLUSHALL -FLUSHDB -DEBUG. Restart Redis after configuration changes.

title: Redis: Protected Mode Disabled
description: Redis protected-mode is disabled. Protected mode is a security layer that rejects connections from external addresses when no authentication is configured and Redis is not bound to specific interfaces. Disabling it removes this safety net.
remediation: Enable protected mode: CONFIG SET protected-mode yes. Persist in redis.conf: protected-mode yes. This is the default setting — only disable if you have both authentication AND interface binding configured. Also bind Redis to specific interfaces: bind 127.0.0.1 <internal_ip>.

title: Redis: Dangerous Commands Not Renamed or Disabled
description: Dangerous Redis commands (FLUSHALL, FLUSHDB, CONFIG, DEBUG, SLAVEOF, REPLICAOF) are not disabled or renamed. An attacker with Redis access can: delete all data (FLUSHALL), reconfigure Redis to write to arbitrary files (CONFIG SET dir / CONFIG SET dbfilename), or initiate replication to an attacker-controlled server for data exfiltration.
remediation: In redis.conf, rename or disable dangerous commands: rename-command FLUSHALL ''. rename-command FLUSHDB ''. rename-command CONFIG ''. rename-command DEBUG ''. rename-command SLAVEOF ''. rename-command REPLICAOF ''. For Redis 6+ ACLs: ACL SETUSER default off; ACL SETUSER appuser on ><pass> +@read +@write -CONFIG -FLUSHALL -FLUSHDB -DEBUG.

title: Redis: CONFIG Command Accessible to Non-Admin Users
description: The Redis CONFIG command is accessible and can be used to change server configuration at runtime including: the data directory (dir) and RDB filename, enabling replication to an attacker server, and disabling authentication. CONFIG SET dir and CONFIG SET dbfilename have been used to write SSH authorized_keys files and crontabs.
remediation: Disable or rename the CONFIG command: rename-command CONFIG ''. For Redis 6+ use ACLs to restrict CONFIG to admin users only. Monitor CONFIG command usage in slowlog and audit logs. If CONFIG is needed for operational purposes, implement it via a privileged management interface only.

title: Cassandra: AllowAllAuthenticator Configured (No Authentication)
description: Cassandra is configured with AllowAllAuthenticator, which means authentication is completely disabled. Any client connecting to the CQL port can execute any query on any keyspace without credentials.
remediation: Change authenticator to PasswordAuthenticator in cassandra.yaml: authenticator: PasswordAuthenticator. Also change authorizer to CassandraAuthorizer: authorizer: CassandraAuthorizer. After enabling auth, the default cassandra/cassandra credentials must be changed immediately. Restart all nodes in a rolling fashion.

title: Cassandra: Default cassandra/cassandra Credentials in Use
description: Cassandra is using the default superuser credentials (cassandra/cassandra). These credentials are well-known and the first attempted by attackers. The cassandra superuser has full access to all keyspaces and the ability to create/modify users.
remediation: Change the default cassandra password immediately: ALTER USER cassandra WITH PASSWORD '<new_strong_password>'; Create a new named superuser account: CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD '<password>' SUPERUSER; Optionally disable the default cassandra account: ALTER USER cassandra NOSUPERUSER.

title: Cassandra: Client-to-Server Encryption Disabled
description: Cassandra client_encryption_options.enabled is set to false. All CQL traffic between clients and Cassandra nodes is transmitted in cleartext, including authentication credentials.
remediation: Enable client encryption in cassandra.yaml: client_encryption_options: enabled: true optional: false keystore: <path_to_keystore> keystore_password: <password> require_client_auth: false store_type: JKS. Set optional: false to require TLS for all connections.

title: Cassandra: JMX Remote Access Without Authentication
description: Cassandra JMX remote access is enabled without authentication (LOCAL_JMX=no in cassandra-env.sh but JMX_AUTH or JMX_PASSWORD not configured). JMX provides full management access including schema modifications, compaction control, and the ability to expose all Cassandra internals.
remediation: Enable JMX authentication in cassandra-env.sh: com.sun.jndi.rmi.object.trustURLCodebase=false, JVM_OPTS="$JVM_OPTS -Dcom.sun.jmx.remote.authenticate=true -Dcom.sun.jmx.remote.password.file=/etc/cassandra/jmxremote.password". Or restrict JMX to localhost: LOCAL_JMX=yes. For Cassandra 4.0+, use the integrated JMX auth.

title: Elasticsearch: Security Features Disabled (X-Pack Security)
description: Elasticsearch X-Pack security features are disabled (xpack.security.enabled: false). Without security enabled, there is no authentication, no authorization, and no TLS. Any client with network access to port 9200 can read all indices, modify data, take snapshots, and access cluster metadata.
remediation: Enable security in elasticsearch.yml: xpack.security.enabled: true. Configure TLS: xpack.security.transport.ssl.enabled: true. Set up built-in user passwords: bin/elasticsearch-setup-passwords auto. This is required for all Elasticsearch deployments since version 8.0 by default, but must be explicitly enabled for 7.x.

title: Elasticsearch: Unauthenticated Cluster Information Exposed
description: The Elasticsearch cluster exposes sensitive information without authentication including: cluster name, node names, version, installed plugins, JVM settings, and index names. This information assists attackers in fingerprinting the deployment and identifying applicable CVEs.
remediation: Enable X-Pack security to require authentication for all API calls. Apply network-level controls (firewall, private VPC) to restrict access to the Elasticsearch API port. If ES must be publicly accessible, ensure security is fully configured and indices containing sensitive data are protected by index-level privileges.

title: Elasticsearch: Snapshot Permissions Not Restricted
description: Elasticsearch snapshot/restore privileges are not properly restricted. Any authenticated user with manage_snapshots or cluster:admin/snapshot/get cluster privileges can create and restore snapshots. Snapshots enable bulk data exfiltration of all index contents to an attacker-controlled repository.
remediation: Restrict snapshot privileges to dedicated backup service accounts only. Use the Elasticsearch security API to create a snapshot role: PUT _security/role/snapshot_manager with only manage cluster privilege on specific repository patterns. Remove snapshot privileges from application service accounts.
validation_notes: Check snapshot permissions: GET _security/role/<role_name>. Test: GET _snapshot/_all (as the service account). If indices are enumerable, check: GET _cat/indices?v for data exposure scope.

title: CouchDB: Admin Party Mode (No Authentication)
description: CouchDB is running in 'Admin Party' mode with no admin account configured. In this mode, everyone has admin access. Anyone with network access to the CouchDB port can create databases, read all data, delete databases, and create admin accounts.
remediation: Create an admin account immediately: curl -X PUT http://localhost:5984/_node/_local/_config/admins/admin -d '"<strong_password>"'. This disables Admin Party mode. Also restrict the bind address to localhost: curl -X PUT http://localhost:5984/_node/_local/_config/httpd/bind_address -d '"127.0.0.1"'.

title: InfluxDB: Authentication Disabled
description: InfluxDB authentication is disabled (auth-enabled=false in influxdb.conf). Any client with network access can query all time-series data, write arbitrary data points, drop measurements, and drop databases without credentials.
remediation: Enable authentication in influxdb.conf: [http] auth-enabled = true. Create an admin user first: CREATE USER admin WITH PASSWORD '<password>' WITH ALL PRIVILEGES. Create application users with database-specific privileges: CREATE USER appuser WITH PASSWORD '<password>'; GRANT READ ON mydb TO appuser.

title: Neo4j: Default Credentials (neo4j/neo4j)
description: Neo4j is accessible using default credentials (neo4j/neo4j). The default credentials are well-known and provide admin access to the graph database including all node/relationship data and the ability to execute Cypher queries and procedures.
remediation: Change the neo4j user password immediately via the browser at :7474 or via cypher-shell: ALTER USER neo4j SET PASSWORD '<strong_password>' CHANGE NOT REQUIRED; Create named user accounts for applications with minimum required roles. Disable the default neo4j account if not needed.

title: Neo4j: Remote Code Execution via APOC Procedures
description: Neo4j APOC (Awesome Procedures on Cypher) library is installed with unrestricted access to system procedures including apoc.load.url (HTTP requests), apoc.load.jdbc (external DB connections), apoc.periodic.submit (background task execution), and file I/O procedures. If an attacker can execute Cypher queries, they can use APOC for SSRF, data exfiltration, and potentially OS access.
remediation: Restrict APOC procedures in neo4j.conf: dbms.security.procedures.whitelist=apoc.coll.*,apoc.load.json. Do not whitelist apoc.load.url, apoc.load.jdbc, apoc.util.sleep, or file-access procedures in production. Apply role-based access control to restrict procedure execution to specific users.
validation_notes: Check installed procedures: CALL dbms.procedures() YIELD name WHERE name STARTS WITH 'apoc' RETURN name; Test specific procedures: CALL apoc.load.url('http://attacker.com') (should fail if restricted).

title: Memcached: No Authentication (SASL Disabled)
description: Memcached is running without SASL authentication (the default). Any client with network access to the Memcached port can read, write, and delete any cached key-value pair. This is particularly dangerous as Memcached often caches session tokens, user data, and application secrets.
remediation: Enable SASL authentication: compile Memcached with --enable-sasl. Configure: -S flag at startup. Create SASL credentials: echo -n 'username:password' > /etc/sasl/memcached. Note: SASL support is compile-time only in standard Memcached. Critically: bind Memcached to localhost only and apply firewall rules as the primary control.

title: Memcached: Exposed to Internet (DDoS Amplification Risk)
description: Memcached is accessible from external network addresses. Publicly accessible Memcached instances (UDP port 11211) have been weaponized for massive DDoS amplification attacks achieving amplification factors of up to 51,000x (CVE-2018-1000115). Any cached data is also readable by anyone on the internet.
remediation: Immediately restrict Memcached to localhost: -l 127.0.0.1 in startup configuration. Disable UDP: -U 0. Apply firewall rules blocking port 11211 from internet. This is a critical operational risk beyond just security — internet-exposed Memcached has been used in record-breaking DDoS attacks.
